Fauxx will perform the following background activities:
Search diverse topics on Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, Yahoo, and Yandex
Visit a variety of websites to broaden your browsing profile
Present a stable per-persona device identity (User-Agent and client hints)

All activity is synthetic and stays on your device. No personal data is collected or transmitted.
An open-source privacy tool that poisons data broker and ad-tech profiles by generating continuous, plausible, off-demographic synthetic activity from your device.
Data that stays on your device

All personal data remains exclusively on your device and is encrypted at rest:

• Demographic profile (age, gender, interests, profession, region)
• Ad platform profile cache (scraped interest categories)
• Synthetic persona history
• Action audit logs

This data is stored in an encrypted database (SQLCipher) with a key managed by Android Keystore. It never leaves your device in any form.

Fauxx generates synthetic browsing activity to confuse tracking profiles. This means the app will:

• Perform web searches on Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, Yahoo, and Yandex
• Visit categorized URLs to accumulate diverse tracker cookies
• Load diverse pages in background web views
• Resolve domain names to generate DNS query noise
• Open app store deep links for off-profile apps

All requests use randomized User-Agent headers and are rate-limited to avoid disrupting target services. Blocked domains (private networks, harmful content) are never contacted.

• No analytics or telemetry of any kind
• No crash reports sent to external services
• No advertising identifiers or tracking pixels
• No server-side accounts or cloud storage
• No data shared with third parties

Fauxx has no backend server. The app is entirely self-contained.

If enabled, the Location Spoofing module feeds synthetic GPS coordinates through Android\'s mock-location provider. Note that this is experimental and largely ineffective today: apps that request location the usual way receive your real location unaffected, and Android marks every mock coordinate so recipients can discard them. It is off by default. See the project README for the measured detail.

You can delete all stored data at any time via Settings > Clear All Data. This permanently removes your demographic profile, platform caches, persona history, action logs, and resets all settings to defaults. Uninstalling the app also removes all data.
Fauxx is open-source software. Source code and license details are available in the project repository.
If you find Fauxx useful, consider buying me a coffee.

I use DuckDuckGo App Tracking Protection or another tracker-blocking app. Does that affect Fauxx?

Yes. Fauxx keeps running, but much of its effect is lost. The decoy signal travels in the requests a page makes to ad networks and analytics companies, and those are exactly what tracker blockers stop. The pages themselves still load, so the log shows normal visits. The Dashboard can usually spot DNS-based blockers (Pi-hole, NextDNS, Private DNS, and the DNS filtering in AdGuard, Rethink or Blokada), and shows a hint when DuckDuckGo is installed and a VPN is on. DuckDuckGo App Tracking Protection itself can't be confirmed from inside Fauxx, so exclude Fauxx from it anyway.

Exclude Fauxx from the blocker. Your other apps stay protected, and what gets through is Fauxx's decoy browsing, not your own.

• DuckDuckGo App Tracking Protection: in its settings, open the list of protected apps and turn protection off for Fauxx.
• Other blocker apps that run as a VPN on your phone (AdGuard, Blokada, Rethink, TrackerControl and similar): add Fauxx to their excluded or bypassed apps. In Rethink, set Fauxx to Exclude: bypass DNS and firewall is not enough on Android 8 to 10, where the system makes Fauxx's DNS lookups on its behalf and Rethink cannot tell they are Fauxx's.
• Blockers that cover your whole network or your phone's DNS (Pi-hole, NextDNS, Private DNS, a router): these can't exclude a single app. Turn on Custom DNS for Fauxx in Settings instead, so Fauxx looks up the sites it visits with a resolver you choose.
Why does Fauxx sometimes stop and show a “Tap to resume protection” notification?

Fauxx voluntarily pauses the engine when one of your configured constraints kicks in:

• Quiet hours: if you have an active-hours window set (default 7am–11pm), Fauxx stops at the end of the window and posts a one-tap notification scheduled for the next start time.
• Network: if your mobile data intensity is set to Off in Settings and Wi-Fi is gone for more than 30 minutes with the screen on, Fauxx releases the foreground-service slot rather than spin idle.
• Battery threshold: if your battery is below the configured threshold and the device isn't charging, Fauxx pauses until the situation changes.

Tapping the notification opens Fauxx and restarts protection. Nothing is lost — your settings, profile, persona, and action log are persistent across pauses.

If you're seeing the engine stop outside of these configured constraints, please file an issue from Settings (“File a GitHub issue”) — that's a bug, not by design.
Why does the dashboard say sites can tell the traffic comes from Fauxx?

Android's WebView adds an X-Requested-With header naming the app to the requests it makes, so every site Fauxx visits could see com.fauxx.full and discard the traffic. Fauxx blanks that header, but only when the installed WebView supports two features, MULTI_PROFILE and CUSTOM_REQUEST_HEADERS. Blanking is not removing: an empty X-Requested-With still goes out, and Chrome itself never sends one, so sites can still tell the traffic comes from an app's WebView, just not that the app is Fauxx. The warning names your WebView, its version and the features it lacks.

Which WebView has them: WebView 151 has both and WebView 113 has neither. The first version in between to have them is not known, so an update may or may not clear the warning.

• With Google Play: update Android System WebView there (on Android 8 and 9 the WebView is usually Chrome, so update Chrome). The warning's button opens its Play page. If it is already up to date, installing its Beta or Dev version from Play and choosing it under Developer options > WebView implementation may get the features sooner, though that is not guaranteed.
• Google's WebView without the Play Store (microG, or Play disabled): it updates from Google Play, so a Play-compatible store such as Aurora Store can update it.
• Other WebViews (de-Googled phones, custom ROMs), for example com.android.webview or a ROM's own build: these usually update with your system or ROM, or from wherever they were installed, such as a ROM's app store or an F-Droid repository. Some ROMs let you choose a different WebView under Developer options > WebView implementation.

For any WebView other than Google Play's, the warning's button opens the WebView's app info so you can see its version.

Fauxx keeps generating activity either way: the warning is about how easily sites can spot that activity. Custom DNS needs a different feature, PROXY_OVERRIDE. WebView 113 and 151 both have it, and Settings says when yours does not.
Why does Fauxx do less, or nothing, while my screen is off?

Android saves battery by putting the phone to sleep when the screen is off, and Fauxx has to work within that:

• Doze: after a while with the screen off, Android holds background work back and lets apps run only now and then. Fauxx wakes the phone for each action, but in deep Doze Android limits how often an app may do that, so actions can be spaced further apart than usual.
• Battery optimization: while Android optimizes Fauxx it can hold the app back much more. Allow unrestricted background usage when the dashboard asks.
• Phone makers' own limits: Samsung, Xiaomi, Huawei, OnePlus and others put apps to sleep on top of Android. On Samsung, set Fauxx's battery usage to Unrestricted and add it to Never sleeping apps (Never auto sleeping apps on newer versions) under Settings > Battery > Background usage limits. If Samsung later suggests putting Fauxx to sleep, decline to keep it running. dontkillmyapp.com has the steps for each brand.
• Your daily rhythm: Fauxx learns the hours you usually use your phone and puts more of its activity there, between half and one and a half times its normal rate, so the noise follows a human pattern. That alone never stops it.
• Active hours: outside the active-hours window in Settings, Fauxx pauses on purpose.

Running overnight costs battery: each action wakes the phone, and at High intensity that can be a couple of hundred times an hour. Low or Medium intensity, or active hours that end at bedtime, keep the cost down.

The debug log (Settings > Export Debug Logs) records each pause with its reason and whether the phone was dozing.
What does “Synthetic Activity” on the Dashboard mean?

It's the average number of decoy actions Fauxx generated per hour over the last 24 hours: how much cover traffic it is adding.

It is NOT a ratio against your real activity, which Android does not let an app see, and it does not measure the quality of the decoys, such as whether they hit categories far from your real interests or fool profiling systems.

To see where the decoy activity is going, check the Targeting screen's category-weight chart. Red bars are categories Fauxx is suppressing (because they match your real profile), green bars are categories it's boosting, gray is neutral. If you have imported an ad profile, the dashboard's Profile Drift card shows how far it has moved from your baseline.
How does Layer 2 (Ad Profile Import) work, and where do I get the export file?

Layer 2 takes the ad-targeting profile that Google and Facebook already keep on you and uses it to steer Fauxx away from your real interests — synthetic activity gets boosted in the OTHER categories.

You export your own data and import the file into Fauxx; no sign-in inside the app, no automated scraping. Android sandboxes cookies per app, so Fauxx genuinely can't see your browser session, and Google + Facebook block sign-in from any embedded WebView, so a “sign in here” flow isn't possible. User-driven export sidesteps both.

How to export:

• Google: there are two ways. In Fauxx, tap “Enter categories from My Ad Center”, open My Ad Center, go to Manage privacy, and copy the list under “Categories used to show you ads” into Fauxx. This is the most complete source, since Google's exports may leave these categories out. Or visit takeout.google.com in your browser, select your advertising data (skip the rest to keep the file small) and request the export; Google emails a download link, usually within minutes. Tap “Import Google Takeout” in Fauxx and pick the .zip.
• Facebook: visit accountscenter.facebook.com, choose Download Your Information → JSON format → “Ads and businesses”. Facebook prepares the archive, emails the link, and you import it via “Import Facebook DYI”.

Things to know:

• Read-only. Fauxx never modifies or interacts with your ad settings on either platform — only reads what's in the export.
• Stays on device. The imported categories are written to the same SQLCipher-encrypted database as the rest of your data. Nothing leaves your phone.
• Refresh cadence is up to you. Re-import whenever you want a fresh snapshot — Fauxx will nudge you with an in-app banner if the last import is over 90 days old (snooze / mute available).
Why doesn\'t Fauxx\'s activity show up in my Google account or My Ad Center?

Because Fauxx is never signed in to your accounts, on purpose. It browses in its own sandboxed WebView with no access to your Google login. Google's terms restrict automated use of its services, and sending Fauxx's decoys through your real account could get that account flagged or suspended.

What you see in My Ad Center, My Activity and Google Takeout comes mostly from what you do while signed in: your searches, YouTube, and Chrome and Android activity tied to your account. Fauxx's activity is not tied to your account, so it will not appear there, and your Google ad interests usually will not change because of it. For the same reason, Profile drift on the Dashboard may barely move for Google.

Fauxx aims at the profiling that needs no login: third-party ad networks and trackers, data brokers, and anything that recognises you by your device, IP address or DNS lookups. Those profiles are not shown to you, so there is no page where you can watch them change.

The Layer 2 import works the other way round. It tells Fauxx what Google and Facebook already think you like, so the decoy personas steer away from your real interests instead of resembling you. It is a baseline for the noise, not a score for whether Fauxx is working.
Does custom DNS cover every lookup Fauxx makes?

Almost, and you choose what happens when it can't.

With Custom DNS on, every site Fauxx's browser loads, including the images, scripts and ads inside a page, is looked up through your resolver: Fauxx's WebView hands each name to Fauxx's own proxy, which asks your resolver.

Two things still use your device's DNS by default:

• Fallback. If your resolver is slow or unreachable (three slow or failed lookups in a row, which happens easily over a VPN), Fauxx sends lookups to your device's DNS for at least a minute, then tries your resolver again, and says so on the dashboard. Turn on Settings → Never fall back to your device's DNS to stop this: lookups then fail, and Fauxx's pages don't load until your resolver answers again.
• DNS noise. Its lookups go to your device's DNS on purpose, to fill your network's and ISP's DNS logs. Turn on Also use it for DNS noise to send them to your resolver; Never fall back to your device's DNS does this too while it is on.

Your own resolver can use http:// if it is on a private network: give its private IP address, or use a name ending in .lan, .local, .home.arpa, .internal or .ts.net. Its lookups are then not encrypted, and they go out on whatever network your phone is on, including public Wi-Fi that uses the same private addresses. A 100.x (Tailscale) or VPN address only reaches your server while that VPN is connected.

Other apps, and Android itself, keep using your device's DNS: custom DNS covers Fauxx's own traffic only.

This resolver uses http://, so its lookups are not encrypted. Fauxx sends them on whatever network your phone is on, including public Wi-Fi that happens to use the same private addresses, where anyone on it can read them. A 100.x (Tailscale) or VPN address only reaches your server while that VPN is connected. With Never fall back to your device\'s DNS on, also enter the server\'s IP address.

If a VPN or firewall app filters DNS, exempt Fauxx from its DNS filtering (in Rethink, choose Exclude for Fauxx; if your resolver is only reachable through Rethink, set Fauxx to bypass DNS and firewall instead); otherwise it may block Fauxx\'s encrypted DNS, or the connections made with its answers. But if your resolver is only reachable through that VPN, do not exempt Fauxx from the VPN itself. This gets around DNS-level blocking only, not blocking by IP address. While it is on, sites that support HTTP/3 are reached over HTTP/2. If custom DNS stops working, Fauxx falls back to your device\'s DNS and says so on the dashboard, unless Never fall back to your device\'s DNS is on.

Something on this phone is blocking the trackers Fauxx\'s decoys need to reach, most likely a tracker-blocking or VPN app such as DuckDuckGo App Tracking Protection. Exclude Fauxx from it.

Something on this phone or network is blocking the trackers Fauxx\'s decoys need to reach, most likely DNS filtering (Pi-hole, NextDNS, Private DNS). Exclude Fauxx from it where you can, or turn on Custom DNS for Fauxx in Settings.
Fauxx\'s requests to trackers are being blocked even with Custom DNS for Fauxx on, so its decoys aren\'t reaching them. The resolver you chose may filter trackers; pick one that doesn\'t.

Something on this phone or network is cutting off the trackers Fauxx\'s decoys need to reach, most likely a firewall on your network or router. Exclude Fauxx from it where you can. Custom DNS won\'t help with this kind of blocking.
DuckDuckGo App Tracking Protection may be blocking the trackers Fauxx\'s decoys need to reach. If it\'s on, exclude Fauxx from it.
